findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2026/2026
findings.headline: Interest rate forecasts proved significantly wrong; rates remained above 5% when the council anticipated gradual cuts, creating uncertainty about future borrowing costs.
findings.detail: The council forecast rate reductions throughout 2025/26 starting in June, but actual cuts began in April and rates stayed elevated through March 2026. The report now expresses uncertainty about future rates, noting market expectations are 'heavily influenced by the conflict in the Middle East.' This undermines the financial case for deferring borrowing, which assumed lower rates would be available when reserves run out.
findings.matters: The council's strategy depends on being able to borrow at lower rates in future; if rates remain elevated when reserves deplete, costs will be higher than planned and could worsen the financing ratio.
findings.figures: PWLB borrowing rates remained above 5% through March 2026. Bank of England rate held at 3.75% on 30 April 2026.
findings.quote: Interest rate forecasts initially suggested gradual reductions in short, medium and long term borrowing rates during 2025/26, however, this did not transpire as markets expected. By March 2026 borrowing rates were at elevated levels due to inflation concerns arising primarily from global events.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2026/2026
findings.headline: Investment balances fell £51m year-on-year because the council used reserves to fund capital programmes instead of borrowing externally.
findings.detail: Available funds for investment dropped from a £281m average during the year to £230m by 31 March 2026. The council states this was deliberate: using reserves to advance capital expenditure rather than accessing external borrowing at current rates. This is a finite strategy—reserves cannot sustain capital funding indefinitely, and the council will eventually need to borrow or cut capital spending.
findings.matters: Lenders view reserve depletion as erosion of financial resilience; when driven by avoidance of borrowing rather than improved performance, it signals medium-term stress.
findings.figures: Investment balances: £281m average during 2025/26, £230m actual at 31 March 2026.
findings.quote: The main reason for the decrease in funds available by the end of the year is a result of using reserves and balances to help fund the capital programme, in advance of using borrowing to finance this expenditure.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2026/2026
findings.headline: General Fund financing costs reached 8.6% of revenue outturn, significantly above the revised budget of 7.0%, leaving less flexibility to handle pressures.
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream came in at 8.6% actual versus 7.0% revised estimate—a 23% overshoot. This means nearly 8.6p of every pound of revenue is locked into debt service. The council's own guidance notes that higher ratios mean reduced ability to shift resources to priorities or absorb funding shortfalls, indicating tighter financial flexibility than planned.
findings.matters: Lenders assess financial flexibility through this ratio; a higher-than-expected ratio indicates less capacity to manage future pressures and suggests the council is more heavily committed to debt service than anticipated.
findings.figures: General Fund ratio: 7.7% originally estimated, 7.0% revised, 8.6% actual.
findings.quote: The higher the ratio, the lower the flexibility there is to shift resources to priority areas and/or reduce expenditure to meet funding shortfalls.

findings.paper_title: City Centre North regeneration
findings.headline: Scheme depends heavily on securing external grant funding, primarily from Homes England, to viability
findings.detail: The Finance Director indicates that securing sufficient grant support from funding authorities will be essential to close the funding gap. Homes England is identified as 'the most likely funders of sufficient scale' to contribute. The council is not yet certain of the level of funding available or whether it will be secured.
findings.matters: External funding gaps that depend on another public body's discretionary grants represent contingency risk for the council's capital plan
findings.figures: No specific figures for grant required provided; to be 'robustly tested through a developer led business case'
findings.quote: It is expected that Homes England would be the most likely funders of sufficient scale to contribute towards any funding gap

findings.paper_title: City Centre North regeneration
findings.headline: Council may need to fund regeneration gaps from general capital resources if external funding falls short
findings.detail: If delivery options contain residual funding gaps after exhausting external funding opportunities, these would need to be met from council capital or revenue funds and would compete with all other capital investment priorities. The Finance Director notes this is 'likely to become further challenging as the Council continues the transition into the future Unitary Authority as part of Local Government Reorganisation'.
findings.matters: A lender assessing council creditworthiness needs to understand how much of the council's discretionary capital budget could be absorbed by this single regeneration project
findings.figures: No specific figures for potential gap size provided; decision point in early 2027 when business case is returned to Cabinet
findings.quote: If the delivery options ultimately contain residual funding gaps, and all other funding opportunities have been exhausted, in order to progress, these would need to be provided from Council funds (capital or revenue) and would naturally be in competition with all of Capital Investment priorities of the City Council. This is likely to become further challenging as the Council continues the transition into the future Unitary Authority as part of Local Government Reorganisation

findings.paper_title: City Centre North regeneration
findings.headline: City centre regeneration scheme has already consumed £18.67m and faces considerable identified funding gaps
findings.detail: The council has spent £18.67m to date on the scheme, including £11.01m on land acquisition (Delancey Assets). The Finance Director's report explicitly identifies that delivery options are likely to result in 'considerable residual funding gaps both for the early and longer-term phases'. A further Cabinet report in early 2027 will set out the final business case and capital funding requirement.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the total exposure of council resources to this regeneration commitment and whether the funding gap poses a risk to the council's financial position
findings.figures: £18.67m spent to date; £2.18m remaining approved funding; up to £250,000 for professional fees under the DMSA; additional capital funding to be bid for in the 2027/28-2029/30 capital bids process
findings.quote: early estimates suggest that the delivery options outlined in the appendices are likely to result in considerable residual funding gaps both for the early and longer-term phases of delivery

findings.committee: Cabinet Member for Children, Families and Education
findings.paper_title: Dedicated Schools Grant Outturn 2025-26 and Revised Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: No contingency for further High Needs growth in 2026-27 despite ongoing demand pressures
findings.detail: The council states that 'unlike previous years, no allowance has been made for further in-year increases' to the High Needs budget in 2026-27, despite continuing to see increasing EHCP assessment requests and higher levels of need. The paper commits to 'close monitoring' but has removed the budget buffer that previously absorbed in-year growth.
findings.matters: Removing contingency for known, continuing demand pressures increases the risk of further mid-year overspends, which the depleting carry-forward balance cannot absorb.
findings.figures: High Needs block base allocation for 2026-27: £52.721m (later revised to £51.720m). No additional growth contingency built in despite £1.822m overspend in 2025-26 and £1.737m overspend on Element 3 specifically.
findings.quote: As previously reported the increase in the levels of need seen up to December 2025 has been built into the 2026-27 budget, but unlike previous years, no allowance has been made for further in-year increases. Close monitoring of this budget will continue in 2026-27.

findings.committee: Cabinet Member for Children, Families and Education
findings.paper_title: Dedicated Schools Grant Outturn 2025-26 and Revised Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Carry-forward balance falling from £11.1m to £8.0m and projected to turn negative in 2026-27
findings.detail: The DSG brought-forward balance decreased by £3.1m from March 2025 (£11.126m) to March 2026 (£8.014m). In 2026-27, planned commitments total £9.530m (including £8.528m for the High Needs shortfall) against only £8.014m available, creating a projected deficit of £1.516m that must be covered.
findings.matters: Reliance on declining reserves to fund ongoing structural deficits signals that the council's position is unsustainable and risks exhausting its buffer for other pressures or emergencies.
findings.figures: Brought forward 2024-25: £11.126m. Brought forward 2025-26: £8.014m. Deficit in 2026-27 before revisions: £1.516m (revised to £515k after budget adjustments but still in deficit).
findings.quote: The DSG carry forward has provided funding to support the shortfall in the High Needs DSG for 2026-27 along with specific projects for the agreed duration.

findings.committee: Cabinet Member for Children, Families and Education
findings.paper_title: Dedicated Schools Grant Outturn 2025-26 and Revised Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: High Needs block overspent by £1.8m in 2025-26 and faces an £8.5m shortfall in 2026-27
findings.detail: The High Needs budget overspent by £1.822m in 2025-26, driven by a £1.737m overspend on Element 3 Top-up funding (EHCP support in special schools, inclusion centres and post-16 colleges) and a £692k overspend on out-of-city placements. The council budgeted for the High Needs shortfall in 2026-27 to be £8.528m, which must be covered from carry-forward reserves.
findings.matters: A persistent structural deficit in a major service function, funded by depleting one-off reserves, indicates the council may eventually face difficult choices about provision levels or will require general fund support despite DSG being ring-fenced.
findings.figures: 2025-26 High Needs overspend: £1.822m. Element 3 Top-up overspend: £1.737m. Out of City Placements overspend: £0.692m. 2026-27 High Needs shortfall to be funded from reserves: £8.528m.
findings.quote: The authority continues to see increasing numbers of requests for Education Health and Care Plan (EHCP) assessments and growth in levels of need, particularly within Special Schools, Inclusion centres and post-16 colleges, which has led to the net overspend for 2025-26

findings.paper_title: 26 PCC - Audit Planning Report - June 2026 - FINAL_
findings.headline: Quality of working papers and supporting evidence inadequate; audit required multiple rounds of queries on significant balances
findings.detail: The 2024/25 audit found that the council's quality of working papers and supporting evidence required improvement. Specific issues included incomplete explanations, insufficient third-party evidence for balance verification (particularly for Debtors, Creditors, and Grants Receipts in Advance), and multiple rounds of queries needed to obtain supporting documentation. For IFRS 16 leases, a new standard in 2024/25, the audit team had to undertake multiple rounds of cleansing and review to obtain a comprehensive list of items.
findings.matters: Weak working paper quality and incomplete audit evidence suggests deficiencies in the council's financial management processes and data controls, increasing audit risk and the potential for undetected errors to remain in reported numbers.
findings.figures: Multiple rounds of query and follow-up required; specific areas: Debtors, Creditors, Grants Receipts in Advance, and IFRS 16 lease documentation
findings.quote: We did experience issues with the support provided for some specific areas of our testing, including Debtors, Creditors and Grants Receipts in Advance. In these cases, many of our samples were returned without complete explanations or sufficient third party evidence to support the balances, resulting in multiple rounds of returning queries and follow-up with Management.

findings.paper_title: 26 PCC - Audit Planning Report - June 2026 - FINAL_
findings.headline: Major regeneration asset (Lakeside North Harbour, £111.2m) creates 11% materiality exposure and requires annual valuation challenge
findings.detail: The Lakeside North Harbour office complex, purchased in 2019 as part of regeneration policy, is valued at £111.2m and is the council's second-largest property asset. It requires significant judgmental inputs for valuation through existing use value. The auditors note that a misstatement of less than 11% would exceed their performance materiality threshold of £10.7m, creating material exposure to balance sheet risk.
findings.matters: An asset representing 11% of performance materiality creates material exposure if valuation is incorrect. The council's regeneration strategy depends on the Lakeside asset performing and holding value; any significant impairment would materially affect reported financial position and borrowing ratios.
findings.figures: Lakeside asset valued at £111.2m; performance materiality £10.7m; 11% error would exceed materiality; asset purchased August 2019
findings.quote: The Lakeside site was purchased in August 2019 and continues to be highly material to the financial statements, with a valuation in the prior year of £111.2m. A misstatement of less than 11% of the asset value would exceed our performance materiality.

findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing judgment on council's housing arrangements: significant improvement needed in consumer standards
findings.detail: The council made a self-referral to the Regulator of Social Housing and received a regulatory judgment stating that 'consumer standards and significant improvement is needed'. The auditors have identified this as a risk of significant weakness in governance arrangements requiring follow-up during the 2025/26 audit, with planned procedures to review the council's improvement actions.
findings.matters: A regulatory judgment indicating that significant improvement is needed in consumer standards represents a material governance and operational risk. For a lender, this signals both service delivery deficiencies and the reputational/operational costs of remediation.
findings.figures: One regulatory judgment on social housing standards; council holds housing stock valued at £838m
findings.quote: A risk of significant weakness has been identified relating to the Self Referral to the Regulator of Social Housing and Subsequent Regulatory Judgement.

findings.paper_title: 26 PCC - Audit Planning Report - June 2026 - FINAL_
findings.headline: Uncorrected material £30 million prior year PPE valuation adjustment leaves balance sheet misstated
findings.detail: In 2024/25 audit testing, auditors identified a prior year adjustment of approximately £30 million relating to PPE valuations. A group of assets should have been revalued using Depreciated Replacement Cost in 2023/24 but were not. The auditors assessed this misstatement as material to the accounts, yet management chose not to correct it in the 2024/25 comparatives.
findings.matters: An uncorrected material misstatement of £30m indicates deficiencies in the council's asset valuation processes and suggests the balance sheet may not reflect the true position of a major asset class (representing 4% of gross expenditure of £713m).
findings.figures: £30 million adjustment; represents ~4% of gross expenditure
findings.quote: Management have confirmed that they will not be adjusting for this misstatement within the 2023/24 comparatives in the 2024/25 Statement of Accounts. This misstatement is material to the Accounts and therefore this will impact the wording of the opinion given.

findings.paper_title: 26 PCC - Audit Planning Report - June 2026 - FINAL_
findings.headline: Qualified audit opinion in 2024/25 following a disclaimed opinion in 2023/24 indicates persistent deficiencies in financial reporting and internal control
findings.detail: The council received a qualified audit opinion in 2024/25 following a disclaimed opinion in 2023/24. The auditors describe the council as being in 'Phase 2' of rebuilding assurance toward an unqualified opinion. The 2024/25 audit identified multiple preparedness weaknesses: working papers and supporting evidence quality 'requires improvement', the 'volume and value of identified misstatements' 'requires improvement', and multiple misstatements across disclosure notes including Note 2, Note 8, Note 12, Note 17, Note 37 and Note 39.
findings.matters: A qualified or disclaimed audit opinion indicates significant deficiencies in the council's financial controls and accounting practices, making it materially harder for a lender to rely on reported financial position and asset values.
findings.figures: 2023/24: disclaimed opinion; 2024/25: qualified opinion; Working papers quality and misstatement volume both rated 'requires improvement'
findings.quote: Management has overall responsibility for leading and sustaining the Council's recovery from a disclaimed audit opinion.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 25-26
findings.headline: General Fund financing cost ratio increased to 8.6%, significantly above the revised estimate of 7.0%
findings.detail: The actual ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream for the General Fund reached 8.6%, exceeding the revised estimate of 7.0% (and original estimate of 7.7%). This means 8.6% of the council's revenue stream is committed to financing debt, leaving less flexibility to shift resources or manage funding shortfalls. The paper does not explain the 1.6 percentage point variance between revised and actual.
findings.matters: A higher-than-expected financing cost ratio indicates the council's revenue situation is tighter than anticipated. This reduces flexibility for the council and suggests either revenue underperformance or unaccounted financing costs.
findings.figures: Actual ratio 8.6%; Revised estimate 7.0%; Original estimate 7.7%; variance of 1.6 percentage points
findings.quote: This ratio reflects the annual cost of financing net debt as a proportion of the total revenue financing received. It therefore represents the proportion of the City Council's expenditure that is largely fixed and committed to repaying debt. The higher the ratio, the lower the flexibility there is to shift resources to priority areas and/or reduce expenditure to meet funding shortfalls.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 25-26
findings.headline: Interest rate environment shifted; rates no longer expected to fall, may rise instead
findings.detail: Initial forecasts expected the Bank Rate to fall to around 3.25% by mid-2026, but this is now considered unlikely. As of the Bank of England meeting on 30 April 2026, rates are held at 3.75% and are 'not anticipated to be cut further for some time, and may in fact be increased in the coming months to counteract inflationary pressures from rising energy costs.' This undermines the business case for the internal borrowing strategy, which depends on external rates staying elevated.
findings.matters: The council's strategy to draw down reserves rather than borrow externally was predicated on elevated rates staying in place. If rates fall or stabilize lower than expected, the council will have depleted reserves unnecessarily while external borrowing becomes cheaper.
findings.figures: Bank Rate started 2025/26 at 4.5%; three 0.25% cuts brought it to 3.75% by year-end; forecast cut to 3.25% now considered unlikely
findings.quote: However, since March 2026, the steady reduction in the Bank Rate, which was expected to continue into 2026/27 before settling at a rate of around 3.25%, is now considered unlikely due to a growing concerns over higher inflation. As a result interest rates are not anticipated to be cut further for some time, and may in fact be increased in the coming months to counteract inflationary pressures from rising energy costs.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 25-26
findings.headline: Council maintaining £292m internal borrowing using reserves instead of external borrowing at elevated rates
findings.detail: The Council has a Capital Financing Requirement of £1,010m but actual gross debt of only £718m, with the £292m gap covered by internal borrowing using reserves, balances and cash. This strategy avoids borrowing at rates above 5%, but the report explicitly notes it 'requires ongoing monitoring as the underlying need to borrow increases.' As the CFR grows, reserves will eventually deplete and external borrowing will become necessary.
findings.matters: For a lender, reserve depletion is a material risk. The strategy depends on having sufficient reserves available and on rates remaining elevated; as the underlying borrowing need increases, this becomes unsustainable.
findings.figures: Capital Financing Requirement £1,010m; Gross debt £718m; Internal borrowing £292m; Elevated borrowing rates >5%
findings.quote: During 2025/26, the Council continued to maintain an under-borrowed position and no new borrowing was undertaken. The Council's underlying need to borrow (the Capital Financing Requirement) was £1,010m on 31 March 2026, and was not fully funded with loan debt since, as mentioned, the Council's actual gross debt of £718m was being maintained at a lower level by using cash supporting the authority's reserves, balances and cash flow as an interim measure. This is also termed "Internal Borrowing" and amounted to £292m by 31 March 2026. This strategy is a prudent and cost-effective approach in the current economic climate while the rate at which new borrowing can be obtained remains at elevated levels (>5%) and near-term investment rates have generally been lower. However, it requires ongoing monitoring as the underlying need to borrow increases.

Resources have not yet been recruited to enable completion and annual refresh of surveys. findings.matters: Asbestos compliance failure creates material health and safety liability exposure and affects asset valuations; the recruitment backlog indicates governance weakness in managing critical compliance risks

findings.detail: The Data Governance audit raised 4 high-risk exceptions: outdated policies, Information Asset Registers not being maintained, council-wide mandatory training compliance at only 76%, and gaps in corporate oversight due to resourcing constraints. findings.detail: The Rental Income audit identified absence of formal arrears management policy, write-offs processed with limited supporting evidence, credit adjustments without proper authorisation or audit trails, credit balances not consistently monitored, and refunds with incomplete documentation. All findings are high-risk. Agreed actions are scheduled to be implemented by December 2026.

This deficit depends on achieving planned savings. Internal audit also highlighted key areas of income collection, high demand, and financial process where the authority is not achieving value for money.
findings.matters: A structural deficit that depends on planned savings represents a material financial stability risk for lenders; if savings are not delivered on schedule, the council faces a budget crisis

findings.paper_title: Portico Holdings Ltd 2026/27 budget and 2027/28 to 2028/29 forecast
findings.headline: Budget forecast depends on planned contributions from Portsmouth City Council, suggesting Portico may not be fully self-sustaining.
findings.detail: The Director of Finance notes that the forecast budgeted profit/loss is consistent with "planned contributions from the City Council" included in the Council's February 2026 budget. This language suggests ongoing council subsidy or grant support, not pure commercial operation.
findings.matters: If Portico requires recurring council contributions (beyond debt service), it is not a self-financing investment and council lending is effectively funding recurring losses.
findings.figures: Not specified in main document; detail in exempt Appendix 1
findings.quote: The forecast 'Budgeted (Profit)/Loss' shown in Appendix 1 of Appendix A is consistent with the planned contributions from the City Council which were included within the budget approved by the City Council in February 2026.

findings.paper_title: Portico Holdings Ltd 2026/27 budget and 2027/28 to 2028/29 forecast
findings.headline: £4.8m Freeport SEED grant funding will partially offset capital requirement but carries completion risk with December 2026 target.
findings.detail: Portico has secured external grant funding for cargo terminal redevelopment. Completion is targeted for end of 2026. This reduces council capital burden but project delivery risk exists.
findings.matters: External funding de-risks the council's capital requirement and improves project economics, but delay would increase council drawdown pressure.
findings.figures: £4.8 million Freeport SEED grant; expected completion end of 2026
findings.quote: The Company has been successful in securing £4.8 million of Freeport SEED grant funding which will support the redevelopment of the cargo terminal

findings.paper_title: Portico Holdings Ltd 2026/27 budget and 2027/28 to 2028/29 forecast
findings.headline: Operational land shortage limits growth despite £9.9m capital programme and constrains ability to capture market opportunity.
findings.detail: Portico continues to suffer from insufficient operational land to support deep-water berths. Prospect Road land transfer (planned for 2023) was significantly delayed but finally completed in late 2025. The constraint limits hinterland capacity even as the company invests in terminal redevelopment.
findings.matters: Capital investment productivity depends on ability to use it operationally; land constraints may limit revenue upside and extend payback period.
findings.figures: Transfer completed late 2025 (significant delay from planned 2023); company notes need for "suitable hinterland to support operations"
findings.quote: The Company continues to suffer from lack of available operational land to support the deep water berths.

findings.paper_title: Portico Holdings Ltd 2026/27 budget and 2027/28 to 2028/29 forecast
findings.headline: Portico required external restructuring after independent review in 2024 and remains in second year of turnaround plan.
findings.detail: An independent external consultant review in 2024 prompted restructuring. This is the second budget approval under the new plan. While the review concluded continued council investment was the best option, the need for formal restructuring signals prior underperformance.
findings.matters: A lender should understand whether management and board changes have been effective and whether turnaround risks have been resolved or merely deferred.
findings.figures: Independent review completed in 2024; restructuring implemented; 2026/27 is second budget under new plan
findings.quote: This is the second budget for approval following a full independent review of the company by external consultants in 2024.

findings.paper_title: Portico Holdings Ltd 2026/27 budget and 2027/28 to 2028/29 forecast
findings.headline: Portico's cargo forecast carries significant volatility risk from Brexit-related trading disruptions and Border Control Post uncertainty.
findings.detail: The company is exposed to market swings in fruit trade and EU transhipment volumes. UK-EU Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures agreements and uncertainty around the Border Control Post continue to impact forecasting. The Company Advisory Group explicitly noted "cargo forecast summary included some risk due to the volatility of the current state of trade."
findings.matters: If cargo volumes fall short of forecast, revenue declines and the company's ability to repay council loans or reduce subsidy requirements is jeopardised.
findings.figures: Not quantified in main document; forecasts in exempt appendices
findings.quote: The business is sensitive to market conditions and commercial volatility e.g., fruit trade and changes to EU trading conditions impacting on transhipment of deep-sea cargo to EU (removing the need for landing cargo in the UK).

findings.paper_title: Portico Holdings Ltd 2026/27 budget and 2027/28 to 2028/29 forecast
findings.headline: Portsmouth must fund £9.9m of capital investment in Portico over three years from existing loan facility.
findings.detail: Cabinet is asked to note Portico's capital requirement of £9.9m over 2026/27–2028/29, funded by council loan. The council agreed to increase the loan facility from £15m to £28.6m in October 2024; by March 2026, £16.5m had been drawn, leaving £12.1m available drawdown.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the scale and certainty of council commitments to a trading subsidiary, and whether a £28.6m facility was adequately stress-tested.
findings.figures: £9.9 million capital requirement; £28.6m total loan facility (increased from £15m in October 2024); £16.5m drawn by March 2026; £12.1m remaining drawdown balance
findings.quote: Notes Portico's capital requirement over the 2026/27 to 2028/29 period of £9.9 million, funded by a Council loan, which is within the Council's existing Capital Programme

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Policy 2026/2027
findings.headline: Large investment portfolio (£176m) with strict sector and geographic limits reflecting treasury's risk appetite and refinancing concerns
findings.detail: The council holds £176m in investments as of 1 April 2026 against £697m debt. Treasury management policy imposes significant concentration limits: £80m maximum in money market funds, £155m in building societies, £60m in Eurozone investments, £50m in pooled investment vehicles. These constraints suggest heightened concern about liquidity and credit risk, particularly as the council transitions to accessing markets for funding.
findings.matters: Investment portfolio composition and concentration limits indicate how treasury manages credit and liquidity risk; large investment holdings with restricted maneuverability affect cash management during refinancing periods
findings.figures: £176m investments (1 April 2026); £80m money market fund limit; £155m building societies limit; £60m Eurozone limit; £50m pooled vehicles limit; £31.2m annual treasury management budget
findings.quote: The Council's investments on 1 April 2026 are estimated to be £176m. The cost of the Council's borrowings and the income derived from the Council's short-term treasury investments are included within the Council's treasury management budget of £31.2m for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Policy 2026/2027
findings.headline: Council may require up to £60m additional borrowing in 2026/27 for early Local Government Pension Scheme contribution payments
findings.detail: The council is evaluating an early pension payment of three years' contributions to Hampshire Local Government Pension Scheme. If taken, this would require up to £60m external borrowing beyond the planned capital financing borrowing. The repayment strategy assumes funds will be recovered from pension contributions saved by making the early payment.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities represent contingent obligations; large lump sum payments indicate either liability concerns or opportunistic use of reserves; either carries implications for financial stability
findings.figures: Up to £60m additional borrowing required; financing through monthly pension contribution savings; separate from capital programme borrowing
findings.quote: In addition, further external borrowing of up to £60m may be required in 2026/27 to enable an early payment, equivalent to 3 years pension contributions, to the Hampshire Local Government Pension Scheme.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Policy 2026/2027
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing significantly from £1,003m to peak of £1,260m by 2029/30, expanding underlying debt burden
findings.detail: The council's total historic capital expenditure requiring future funding (CFR) is expanding materially. The 2026/27 estimate of £1,084m represents an £81m increase from 2025/26, with continued growth peaking at £1,260m in 2029/30. This expanding CFR is the driver of the planned shift to external borrowing and is driven primarily by the capital programme, including investment property enhancements.
findings.matters: Rising CFR indicates growing long-term financial obligations and reduces financial flexibility; lenders assess councils' ability to manage growing debt burdens
findings.figures: CFR £974m (2024/25 actual) to £1,084m (2026/27) to peak of £1,260m (2029/30); Investment Properties element £197m (2026/27), representing 28% of debt for commercial activities
findings.quote: The Council's Capital Financing Requirement (CFR). The CFR is simply the total historic outstanding capital expenditure which has not yet been paid for from either revenue or capital resources.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Policy 2026/2027
findings.headline: HRA and General Fund will shift from reserve-funded to externally-borrowed positions in 2026/27-2027/28 as liquidity cushion erodes
findings.detail: The council is deliberately running an under-borrowed position (using reserves to fund capital expenditure while interest rates are high), but the liability benchmark indicates this strategy must end. The HRA will need external borrowing in 2026/27, the General Fund in 2027/28. Fund balances are declining from £309m (2024/25 actual) to £260m (2026/27 estimate), reducing the reserve buffer available to fund this transition.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand when a council becomes dependent on market access for funding, as this increases refinancing risk and exposure to interest rate movements beyond the council's control
findings.figures: Fund balances £309m (2024/25) declining to £260m (2026/27); currently under-borrowed by £382m (2026/27); HRA external borrowing needed 2026/27, General Fund 2027/28
findings.quote: As the General Fund's liability benchmark gets closer to its existing loan debt, this ability to support the HRA position diminishes suggesting that the HRA will need external borrowing to be taken during 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Revenue & Capital Budget 2026 27 Report Full Council
findings.headline: Between 30 and 40 councils nationally are expected to seek Exceptional Financial Support from central government, indicating systemic pressures across the sector.
findings.detail: The budget preface notes that at the time of writing, financial challenges in local government are expected to drive 30-40 councils to apply for Exceptional Financial Support from central government. This is not additional funding but a temporary measure to enable balanced budgets; any budget gap still needs to be met. This signals Portsmouth is part of a sector-wide crisis.
findings.matters: Portsmouth is not isolated; widespread sector distress increases risk of contagion, reduced market confidence in local government lending, and unpredictable central government bailout frameworks.
findings.figures: 30-40 councils expected to seek Exceptional Financial Support; EFS is temporary measure, not additional funding
findings.quote: the financial challenges faced by Local Government are expected to see between 30 and 40 Councils seeking "Exceptional Financial Support" from Central Government.

findings.paper_title: Revenue & Capital Budget 2026 27 Report Full Council
findings.headline: Business Rate reset removed £5.7m of cumulative growth from Portsmouth, redistributed via Fair Funding formula.
findings.detail: The business rate system was 'reset' in 2026/27 for the first time since 2013/14, removing all business rate growth accumulated since 2013/14 (£5.7m for Portsmouth) and redistributing it across councils according to relative need. This removed local growth incentive and redistributed resources. The council forecasts no net business rate growth assumption going forward to reflect appeal volatility.
findings.matters: Loss of £5.7m in cumulative growth that had been Portsmouth's incentive to generate economic growth, combined with zero-growth forecasts and appeal risk, means this income stream is now volatile and unlikely to improve.
findings.figures: £5.7m cumulative business rate growth removed; Business Rate income for 2026/27 estimated at £68.1m (including £4.0m one-off prior year surplus)
findings.quote: The "Reset" removed all business rate growth from 2013/14 to 2025/26 from every Council (that being £5.7m for Portsmouth City Council) and added it to the funding to be distributed through the Fair Funding Allocation.

findings.paper_title: Revenue & Capital Budget 2026 27 Report Full Council
findings.headline: Council Tax base is 13.7% weaker than average English unitary, limiting income growth and borrowing capacity.
findings.detail: Section 1.11 identifies that Portsmouth has a significantly weaker-than-average council taxbase. The council receives circa £10.7m per annum less in Council Tax than average unitary peers and has 9% lower Council Tax charge. This structural weakness limits the council's capacity to raise revenue through tax increases without crossing referendum thresholds.
findings.matters: Weaker tax capacity means less room to grow revenue through tax increases, making the council more dependent on grant funding (which is volatile) and more exposed to any shortfall in government support.
findings.figures: 13.7% weaker than average English unitary council tax base; £10.7m p.a. less in Council Tax than average unitary peer; 9% lower Council Tax charge
findings.quote: the Council has a significantly weaker-than-average council taxbase (13.7% weaker than the average English unitary).

findings.paper_title: Revenue & Capital Budget 2026 27 Report Full Council
findings.headline: Port Shore Power scheme overspent by £4.3m, consuming corporate capital resources and constraining spending on regeneration and economic priorities.
findings.detail: A capital scheme at the Commercial Ferry Port has overrun by £4.3m, which the budget has had to accommodate within the Capital Programme. This has squeezed available capital funding for new schemes. The 2026/27 budget reflects 'reduced trading surpluses' from the port of £1.4m, adding revenue pressure.
findings.matters: A commercial trading asset (the port) is simultaneously consuming £4.3m of unbudgeted capital, reducing projected trading surpluses by £1.4m, and competing with essential maintenance for limited capital resources.
findings.figures: £4.3m overspend on Shore Power scheme; £1.4m reduction in net trading surplus from Commercial Ferry Port
findings.quote: The Capital Programme for 2026/27 and beyond has accommodated a significant overspending on the Port's Shore Power scheme of £4.3m and, coupled with very substantial building maintenance obligations for the Council's operational estate, leaves the available funding for new Capital Schemes targeted towards new development and improvement priorities extremely limited.

findings.paper_title: Revenue & Capital Budget 2026 27 Report Full Council
findings.headline: Homelessness costs remain £3.7m above 2024/25 levels with no clear reduction strategy identified.
findings.detail: Section 1.8 notes homelessness costs, while not increasing further, remain £3.7m elevated compared to 2024/25 baseline. This is a permanent step-up in the cost base with no savings proposals targeting it. The budget continues to hold contingency provision for temporary accommodation demand.
findings.matters: Persistent £3.7m cost uplift that has not reversed and now forms part of baseline spending reduces the council's financial flexibility and suggests demand-management interventions are not succeeding.
findings.figures: £3.7m above 2024/25 levels (continuing into 2026/27)
findings.quote: Whilst not increasing, Homelessness costs still remain £3.7m above the levels seen in 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: Revenue & Capital Budget 2026 27 Report Full Council
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will cost Portsmouth £15m for implementation in 2028, with further allocations to reserves needed in future years.
findings.detail: Portsmouth's share of the four-unitary mainland reorganisation is estimated at £15m on a population share basis. The budget proposes headroom within the MTRS Reserve to cover internal and agreed external costs during 2026/27, but explicitly notes that further allocations to the MTRS Reserve will be necessary in future years to meet full LGR implementation costs.
findings.matters: A £15m cost emerging during a period of already-forecast deficits and rising social care pressures creates a cliff-edge funding demand that may force further reserve draws or borrowing at a time when financial flexibility is minimal.
findings.figures: £15m implementation cost to Portsmouth City Council (population share basis); Case for Change identified £132m for Four Unitary option across 12 councils
findings.quote: It will be necessary however to consider further allocations to the MTRS Reserve in future years to meet the full costs associated with LGR implementation.

findings.paper_title: Revenue & Capital Budget 2026 27 Report Full Council
findings.headline: Three-year forecast shows £3m deficit from 2027/28 onwards but could swing by ±£6m depending on social care, SEND and inflation volatility.
findings.detail: After balancing 2026/27, the council forecasts £3m cumulative deficit across the next three years, phased as £0.8m, £2.0m, £2.9m. The forecast is explicitly described as 'finely balanced' and highly sensitive to uncontrollable factors: adult and children's social care demand, homelessness, SEND costs, and retained business rate appeals.
findings.matters: A £6m adverse variance from forecast (easily possible given stated uncertainties) would exhaust the minimum £12m General Reserves and force emergency cuts or reserve drawdown mid-term.
findings.figures: £3m cumulative deficit 2027/28-2029/30; potential variance of ±£6m (±£2m p.a.); minimum reserves £12m (4.7% of net spending)
findings.quote: The Forecast is "finely balanced" due to the uncertainty associated with Social Care, SEND and Homelessness, alongside inflation generally and the potential volatility of retained Business Rates due to appeals.

findings.paper_title: Revenue & Capital Budget 2026 27 Report Full Council
findings.headline: DSG deficit of £4.5m will become the council's responsibility after March 2028 when statutory override ends.
findings.detail: The council is setting a DSG budget in deficit for the first time, creating a £4.5m liability. Government has not formally committed to funding any accumulated deficits at March 2028, making it likely Portsmouth will need to fund a proportion from its General Fund. A White Paper on SEND reform is promised but not yet delivered.
findings.matters: This is a £4.5m contingent liability that transfers from central government protection to the council's balance sheet in 2028, potentially requiring drawdown of reserves or service reductions at that date.
findings.figures: £4.5m accumulated deficit by March 2028; statutory override ends March 2028; two-fifths of councils risk Section 114 notices by 2026 due to SEND deficits
findings.quote: it is likely that Local Authorities will need to fund a proportion of any accumulated DSG Deficit as at March 2028. The Council's approach is to prepare a strategy and plan in consultation with the Schools Forum and other partners to work towards a position where there is no overall DSG Deficit by the end of March 2028.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Cover Report and Policy 2026-27
findings.headline: Interest rate timing risk: council deliberately delaying external borrowing while PWLB rates elevated (4.8-6.0%)
findings.detail: PWLB certainty rates are currently 4.8% for 5-year maturity loans and up to 6.02% for 50-year terms (as of 22 Dec 2025). The council is maintaining under-borrowed position to avoid locking in these elevated rates, betting that rates will fall before it needs to borrow. However, the borrowing strategy explicitly acknowledges that rates could rise instead, creating risk of higher long-term capital costs.
findings.matters: This is an explicit timing bet on interest rates. If rates rise before the council borrows in 2027/28+, the cost of capital programmes will increase materially, affecting revenue affordability and forcing prioritisation of capital schemes.
findings.figures: PWLB current rates: 4.81% (5yr), 5.39% (10yr), 6.01% (25yr), 5.78% (50yr maturity). MUFG forecast: 4.10% (5yr), 4.70% (10yr) by end Q4 2027
findings.quote: However, delaying borrowing externally does carry the risk that interest rates may increase resulting in a higher long-term cost of borrowing. The Director of Finance and Resources will monitor interest rates in financial markets and adopt a pragmatic approach to changing circumstances.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Cover Report and Policy 2026-27
findings.headline: General Fund crosses from over-borrowed to under-borrowed position by 2027/28, requiring external borrowing
findings.detail: Currently the General Fund has more external debt (£697m) than indicated by its liability benchmark (need for borrowing). However, existing debt matures annually while the capital programme adds to borrowing needs. By 2027/28, the liability benchmark will exceed outstanding debt, forcing the council to re-enter the market and lock in borrowing rates at whatever level then prevails.
findings.matters: This marks the end of the current under-borrowed phase. The council will lose flexibility and become a regular borrower again from 2027/28. It is consciously delaying borrowing while rates are high, betting on future falls; if rates have risen by 2027/28, it will face higher capital costs.
findings.figures: Currently over-borrowed; liability benchmark crosses existing debt during 2027/28
findings.quote: This leads to a shift from an excess borrowing position to an under borrowed position during 2027/28 when the liability benchmark crosses the outstanding loan debt, suggesting that the General Fund will need to borrow externally at this point.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Cover Report and Policy 2026-27
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account will require external borrowing from 2026/27 as General Fund support diminishes
findings.detail: The HRA has until now been supported by General Fund cash surpluses without needing external borrowing. As the General Fund's financial position tightens (moving from over-borrowed to under-borrowed), this cross-fund support will no longer be available and the HRA will need to access the PWLB for borrowing during 2026/27. A concessionary HRA rate of 0.40% below the General Fund rate is available until 31 March 2027.
findings.matters: This represents a structural break: the HRA will shift from subsidised internal borrowing to market-priced external debt. This increases the cost base and signals the General Fund is no longer in surplus position to provide support.
findings.figures: HRA external borrowing requirement emerging 2026/27; concessionary rate of 0.40% below GF rate available to 31 Mar 2027
findings.quote: This current under-borrowed position has been achieved by surplus funds held by the General Fund being used to support the HRA's loans requirement without the need to take external borrowing. However, as the General Fund's liability benchmark gets closer to its existing loan debt, this ability to support the HRA position diminishes suggesting that the HRA will need external borrowing to be taken during 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Cover Report and Policy 2026-27
findings.headline: Liquid investments depleting rapidly from £252m to £54m as council funds capital from internal cash
findings.detail: Investment balances (liquid resources available to meet cash flow needs) are forecast to fall by 79% from £252m in 2024/25 to £54m by 2026/27, stabilising around £44-50m thereafter. This depletion reflects the council's strategy of maintaining an under-borrowed position and using reserves to fund capital rather than external borrowing.
findings.matters: Declining liquidity buffers reduce financial flexibility to absorb shocks or timing mismatches in capital programmes. This also constrains the council's ability to cross-subsidise other activities, including HRA support.
findings.quote: The application of resources (capital receipts, reserves etc.) to either finance capital expenditure or other budget decisions to support the revenue budget will have an ongoing impact on investments unless resources are supplemented each year from new sources.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Cover Report and Policy 2026-27
findings.headline: Pension scheme early payment requires up to £60m external borrowing in 2026/27, additional to capital programme
findings.detail: The council may borrow up to £60m to make a lump-sum payment of three years' pension contributions to Hampshire Local Government Pension Scheme, rather than paying monthly. This is a one-off decision outside the published capital programme. Debt repayment will be financed from the pension contributions that would otherwise be payable monthly.
findings.matters: This is a material, non-routine borrowing decision that increases 2026/27 debt issuance and creates a fixed debt service obligation. It signals a change in pension funding strategy that affects medium-term financial position.
findings.figures: Up to £60m external borrowing
findings.quote: In addition, further external borrowing of up to £60m may be required in 2026/27 to enable an early payment, equivalent to 3 years pension contributions, to the Hampshire Local Government Pension Scheme. This expenditure is not part of the capital programme and therefore is not included in the tables in this report.

findings.paper_title: Qtr 3 Treasury Management Review 25-26 with Appendix A Final
findings.headline: Investment returns declining with further falls expected for next two years
findings.detail: Council's investment portfolio returned 4.59% annualised over first 9 months of 2025/26, down from 5.16% in prior year. Treasury advisor forecasts continued gradual decline in returns for remainder of this year and the next two years.
findings.matters: Declining investment income compresses the financial returns available to offset borrowing costs. With net interest costs of £8m annually, material compression of investment returns narrows overall financial headroom.
findings.figures: 4.59% current return vs 5.16% prior year, £8.0m net annual interest cost on £445m net debt
findings.quote: investment returns are expected to continue to fall gradually for the remainder of this year and the next two years

findings.paper_title: Qtr 3 Treasury Management Review 25-26 with Appendix A Final
findings.headline: Council financing £305m of capital needs from cash reserves rather than planned borrowing
findings.detail: Capital financing requirement is £1,004m but actual borrowing stands at only £699m, with the £305m gap being met from cash balances. Council states this is cost-effective in current interest rates but explicitly flags that this approach requires ongoing monitoring of cash flows and interest rates to remain prudent and achievable.
findings.matters: Reliance on cash reserves to finance capital reduces liquidity cushion and exposes the council to cash flow risk if capital needs increase or cash balances fall. The council's own emphasis on the need for ongoing monitoring suggests this is a conditional strategy.
findings.figures: £305m from cash balances, £699m borrowing vs £1,004m CFR, net debt £445m
findings.quote: No new borrowing has been taken so far this year and there is currently no intention to borrow for the remainder of 2025/26. This is considered a cost-effective approach in the current economic climate, but cash flows and interest rates require ongoing monitoring to ensure that this remains prudent and achievable.

findings.paper_title: PCC Audit Results Report - Local Government - DRAFT February 2026
findings.headline: Slow responses to audit queries: key governance assurance letters not returned for 9+ months
findings.detail: Assurance letters sent to management, audit committee, internal audit and monitoring officer in April 2025 received responses only in December 2025, January 2026, and February 2026 respectively.
findings.matters: Delayed responses to auditors indicate resource constraints or governance disengagement, both concerning for oversight quality.
findings.figures: 8-10 month delays in returning mandatory audit assurance letters
findings.quote: we do note that of our Assurance Letters sent to Management, TCWG, Internal Audit and the Monitoring Officer in April 2025, only the response from Internal Audit was received by the end of July, as requested. The responses from Management, TCWG and the Monitoring officer were received in December 2025, January 2025 and February 2025, respectively.

findings.paper_title: PCC Audit Results Report - Local Government - DRAFT February 2026
findings.headline: Hilsea Lido revalued as operational despite being non-operational, resulting in £4.0 million overstatement
findings.detail: The Lido was revalued at year-end as a fully operational asset with no obsolescence, but was actually non-operational due to refurbishment works. Capital works in progress were also double-counted in both operational assets and Assets Under Construction.
findings.matters: Significant revaluation error in major council asset indicates valuation process weaknesses and quality control failures.
findings.figures: £4.0 million overstatement (Management adjusted for this)
findings.quote: we identified an issue in the accounting for the valuation of the Hilsea Lido, which was revalued during 2024/25 as a fully operational asset with no obsolescence despite being non-operational at the year end due to significant refurbishment works being undertaken.

findings.paper_title: PCC Audit Results Report - Local Government - DRAFT February 2026
findings.headline: Poor quality of financial accounting evidence and control deficiencies in multiple areas requiring additional audit effort
findings.detail: Auditors experienced widespread issues obtaining complete explanations and third-party evidence for samples, particularly in Debtors, Creditors, and Grants Receipts. Multiple rounds of queries were required. IFRS 16 working papers required extensive cleansing before testing could proceed.
findings.matters: Weak control environment increases the risk of undetected errors and suggests the finance function lacks sufficient capability or resources to maintain accurate records.
findings.figures: Multiple disclosure errors identified, requiring audit extension beyond planned scope
findings.quote: We did experience issues with the support provided for some specific areas of our testing, including Debtors, Creditors and Grants Receipts in Advance. In these cases, many of our samples were returned without complete explanations or sufficient third party evidence to support the balances, resulting in multiple rounds of returning queries and follow-up with Management.

findings.paper_title: PCC Audit Results Report - Local Government - DRAFT February 2026
findings.headline: Multiple unresolved audit misstatements identified but not yet corrected by management
findings.detail: At the time of this draft report, auditors have identified material unresolved misstatements totalling up to £7.1m (including prior year impacts) affecting multiple balance sheet lines. Further misstatements may be identified as audit work continues.
findings.matters: Unresolved audit differences indicate the final accounts may change materially from draft position, creating uncertainty for stakeholders relying on the figures.
findings.figures: £3.7m decrease Non-Current Assets, £2.1m decrease Current Liabilities, £3.1m increase Non-Current Liabilities, £4.7m increase Expenditure (£7.1m including prior year turnaround)
findings.quote: At present, we have identified net uncorrected misstatements which would decrease Non-Current Assets by £3.7 million, decrease Current Liabilities by £2.1 million, increase Non-Current Liabilities by £3.1 million and increase Expenditure by £4.7 million (£7.1 million including the impact of prior year turnaround

findings.paper_title: PCC Audit Results Report - Local Government - DRAFT February 2026
findings.headline: £6.6 million Zero Emission Bus scheme wrongly recorded as a capital asset when council does not own the assets
findings.detail: A £6.6m balance relating to the ZEBRA scheme was held in Assets Under Construction at year-end but should have been recorded as Revenue Expenditure Funded from Capital. Management has agreed it is a misstatement but deferred correction to 2025/26.
findings.matters: This indicates control failures in capital project accounting and deferred correction means the error persists through the reported year-end position.
findings.figures: £6.6 million misclassification
findings.quote: we identified a £6.6 million balance held within AUC at year end which relates to the Zero Emission Bus Regional Area Scheme (ZEBRA). This should have been recorded as Revenue Expenditure Funded from Capital under Statute (REFCUS) as the Council do not own the assets.

findings.paper_title: PCC Audit Results Report - Local Government - DRAFT February 2026
findings.headline: Management refusing to correct a £30 million prior year accounting error in land and buildings valuations
findings.detail: Assets were revalued using Depreciated Replacement Cost in 2024/25 for the first time, but the audit team determined they should have been revalued this way in 2023/24, resulting in a £30m understatement. Management has explicitly refused to adjust the 2023/24 comparatives, and the auditors have flagged this as material to the accounts.
findings.matters: A material misstatement that management refuses to correct indicates governance weakness and raises questions about the accuracy of historical financial data used in lending decisions.
findings.figures: £30 million increase to 2023/24 PPE Balance
findings.quote: This would result in an increase to the 2023/24 PPE Balance of circa £30 million. Management have confirmed that they will not be adjusting for this misstatement within the 2023/24 comparatives in the 2024/25 Statement of Accounts. This misstatement is material to the Accounts and therefore this will impact the wording of the opinion given.

findings.paper_title: PCC Audit Results Report - Local Government - DRAFT February 2026
findings.headline: Council will likely receive a qualified or disclaimed audit opinion, unable to rebuild audit assurance on brought-forward balances
findings.detail: Following a disclaimer of opinion on 2023/24, the auditors have not obtained sufficient evidence to provide a clean opinion on 2024/25. They have no assurance over some brought-forward balances from 2023/24 and cannot rebuild assurance on comparative balances within the audit deadline.
findings.matters: An auditor qualification or disclaimer is a critical red flag for lenders. It signals weaknesses in financial reporting systems and creates uncertainty about the reliability of the council's financial statements.
findings.figures: Backstop date for audit completion: 27 February 2026
findings.quote: we will not be able to rebuild assurance over these balances as part of the 2024/25 audit. We are considering the form of our audit report, and whether we can issue a qualified 2024/25 audit opinion this year rather than a disclaimer.

findings.committee: Cabinet Member for Housing and Tackling Homelessness
findings.paper_title: HRA Budget Report 2026-27 v.4 (3)
findings.headline: Right-to-buy sales surged to 98 in first 9 months of 2025/26, 2–3× the historical average, creating income volatility.
findings.detail: Following a deadline rush under old rules, RTB sales accelerated sharply: 78 sales in the first 9 months of 2025/26 versus a historical average of 27–70 per annum. The paper expects 'an increased level of sales is expected into 2026/27 before any slowdown is anticipated'. This surge is unpredictable and temporary, creating a cliff risk.
findings.matters: RTB sales permanently reduce the rent-generating asset base. A surge followed by normalisation creates income volatility the HRA cannot plan around. This adds uncertainty to already-tight deficit projections.
findings.figures: 78 RTB sales in first 9 months of 2025/26 vs 27–70 per annum historical average; 300 applications ahead of deadline
findings.quote: There was a surge of 300 expressions of interest ahead of the November 2024 deadline for applications under the 'old rules'. This led to 20 sales in the final quarter of 2024/25 and another 78 sales in the first 9 months of 2025/26.

findings.committee: Cabinet Member for Housing and Tackling Homelessness
findings.paper_title: HRA Budget Report 2026-27 v.4 (3)
findings.headline: New business rates (NNDR) charge on HRA car parks added to budget; mitigation strategy not yet developed.
findings.detail: The paper states NNDR costs for HRA car parks were flagged as a risk in the prior year's report and have now materialised in the budget. However, 'Work is underway to mitigate the impact of this cost, and it is planned that a report with proposals will come forward in 2026.' The cost is included in the deficit but no mitigation plan exists yet.
findings.matters: This is a previously-flagged cost now crystallising with no mitigation strategy in place. It adds to the structural deficit and shows reactive rather than proactive financial management.
findings.figures: Amount unspecified in paper; flagged as risk, work ongoing
findings.quote: A budget has now been included for National Non-Domestic Rate (NNDR) costs for HRA Car Parks, which was flagged as a risk for the HRA budget in last year's report. Work is underway to mitigate the impact of this cost, and it is planned that a report with proposals will come forward in 2026.

findings.committee: Cabinet Member for Housing and Tackling Homelessness
findings.paper_title: HRA Budget Report 2026-27 v.4 (3)
findings.headline: Government delayed rent convergence decision until January 2026, eliminating 2026/27 as implementation year.
findings.detail: The government consulted on rent convergence (allowing £1–2 per week additional income on below-formula rents) but delayed the decision to January 2026, after budget-setting deadlines. This pushes implementation to 2027/28 at earliest, losing a year of additional income. The council has 9,000+ tenancies below formula rent worth circa £3m annually if fully converged.
findings.matters: This represents lost income the HRA was planning on. The council cannot generate this revenue itself and is dependent on government policy timing. It also shows the HRA's long-term sustainability relies on policies outside its control.
findings.figures: £3m per annum available if fully converged; 9,000+ tenancies below formula rent; convergence delayed one year
findings.quote: As the decision on rent convergence was delayed until January 2026, it will be difficult to implement for 2026/27 rent setting.

findings.committee: Cabinet Member for Housing and Tackling Homelessness
findings.paper_title: HRA Budget Report 2026-27 v.4 (3)
findings.headline: Employer National Insurance increase of £700k+ only partially compensated by government (£130k), leaving £570k+ net HRA cost.
findings.detail: Government imposed Employer National Insurance contribution increases in 2025/26 with banding changes totalling over £700k to the HRA, but compensation amounted to only £130k (18.5%). This uncompensated £570k+ cost flows directly into the deficit. Staff costs represent circa 25% of all HRA costs, making the council vulnerable to further employment-related policy shocks.
findings.matters: This is an external policy shock the council cannot control or offset. It demonstrates the HRA's exposure to government decisions made with inadequate compensation, and the structural cost of the workforce.
findings.figures: £700k+ NI cost increase; £130k government compensation; net HRA cost £570k+; staff costs ~25% of total
findings.quote: an increase in Employer National Insurance Contributions was announced for 2025/26, along with banding changes, which have increased the HRA costs by over £700,000. The government compensation to local authorities amounted to only £130,000 for the HRA (18.5%).

findings.committee: Cabinet Member for Housing and Tackling Homelessness
findings.paper_title: HRA Budget Report 2026-27 v.4 (3)
findings.headline: Housing service received C3 regulatory judgement for safety and quality failures; compliance very recent.
findings.detail: The housing service self-referred to the regulator in 2024 and received a C3 judgement (below acceptable standard) against the Safety and Quality Standard. A new service delivery model addressing compliance gaps was introduced on 5 January 2026—barely one month before this budget meeting. Monthly improvement meetings are ongoing with the regulator.
findings.matters: A regulatory judgement for safety failures is material credit risk. The very recent timing of the compliance restructure means controls are untested. Ongoing regulatory dialogue signals continued scrutiny and risk of further findings.
findings.figures: C3 judgement issued 2024; remedial service model implemented 5 January 2026; ongoing monthly improvement meetings
findings.quote: In 2024 the housing service self-referred to the regulator of social housing recognising areas where improvements were required to fully comply with the consumer standards. The regulator issued a C3 judgement against aspects of the Safety and Quality Standard.

findings.committee: Cabinet Member for Housing and Tackling Homelessness
findings.paper_title: HRA Budget Report 2026-27 v.4 (3)
findings.headline: Forecast in-year deficits grow to £3.3m by 2029/30, explicitly described as unsustainable.
findings.detail: The 4-year forecast shows escalating in-year deficits: £2.502m (2027/28), £2.590m (2028/29), £3.301m (2029/30). The paper states this trajectory 'is unsustainable in the longer term and is inconsistent with prudent management of the HRA', indicating the council has identified the problem but no solution is presented to arrest the trend.
findings.matters: This shows structural deterioration, not a one-year blip. Reserves will deplete from £25.8m to £16.1m over four years. At the 2029/30 deficit rate, remaining reserves would be exhausted within five more years without intervention.
findings.figures: In-year deficits: 2027/28 £2.502m; 2028/29 £2.590m; 2029/30 £3.301m; reserve depletion circa £12.6m over period
findings.quote: The current forecast, excluding rent convergence, illustrates a draw on reserves over the period of circa £12.6m and an 'in year' deficit of £3.3m in 2029/30 which is unsustainable in the longer term

findings.committee: Cabinet Member for Housing and Tackling Homelessness
findings.paper_title: HRA Budget Report 2026-27 v.4 (3)
findings.headline: The council needs a 6.1% rent increase to break even but is only implementing 4.8%, leaving a structural funding gap.
findings.detail: Modelling shows a 6.1% rent increase would be needed for the HRA to break even, but only the maximum allowed 4.8% increase is being approved. This creates a planned £1.177m deficit in 2026/27 requiring a reserve draw. The gap represents a structural mismatch between costs and income that cannot be closed by policy.
findings.matters: A council unable to balance rents to costs signals either unsustainable service levels or uncontrolled cost inflation. Lenders need to understand whether this gap is temporary or permanent, and how long reserves can sustain it.
findings.figures: 6.1% needed to break even vs 4.8% approved; £1.177m planned deficit for 2026/27; 4.8% increase generates £4.3m
findings.quote: However, the latest modelling indicates that a 6.1% rent increase would be needed to 'break even'.

findings.committee: Cabinet Member for Children, Families and Education
findings.paper_title: Dedicated Schools Grant 2025-2026 Quarter 2 Budget Monitoring
findings.headline: No mitigation plan presented in Q2; council defers mitigation planning to Q3.
findings.detail: The Cabinet Member recommendations acknowledge a £1.4m overspend but note that mitigation plans will be 'considered over the Quarter 2 period' and 'reported at the Quarter 3 period'. This report presents the overspend with explanation but no concrete mitigation actions.
findings.matters: A quarter into the financial year with no mitigation plan for a £1.4m overspend on a ring-fenced budget indicates a lag in response, suggesting the council has not yet identified how to address the structural SEND cost pressures.
findings.figures: £1.4m overspend; no mitigation actions or cost-control options presented
findings.quote: mitigation plans will be considered over the Quarter 2 period to alleviate the forecast in year overspend and will be reported at the Quarter 3 period.

findings.committee: Cabinet Member for Children, Families and Education
findings.paper_title: Dedicated Schools Grant 2025-2026 Quarter 2 Budget Monitoring
findings.headline: DSG carry-forward reserves projected to decline by £5.6m over the financial year, from £11.1m to £5.5m.
findings.detail: Portsmouth brought forward £11.126m in DSG reserves at the start of the year. After accounting for the £1.4m Q2 overspend and other planned uses, the carry-forward balance is forecast to be £5.54m by year-end. The uncommitted balance (after earmarked commitments) is forecast at just £4.662m.
findings.matters: Ring-fenced DSG budgets cannot be supplemented from general fund reserves. Rapid depletion of the buffer signals the council is consuming its capacity to absorb future SEND cost inflation; if overspends persist, it faces a DSG deficit requiring government approval.
findings.figures: Reserves declining £5.586m over one financial year; brought forward £11.126m; year-end forecast £5.54m; uncommitted balance £4.662m
findings.quote: As at the end of September 2025, the carry forward balance is projected to be £4.6m a reduction of £0.5m from Quarter 1 monitoring.

findings.committee: Cabinet Member for Children, Families and Education
findings.paper_title: Dedicated Schools Grant 2025-2026 Quarter 2 Budget Monitoring
findings.headline: Post-16 college cost inflation with further unquantified rate increase requests from other providers.
findings.detail: City of Portsmouth College rates have increased (with increases backdated to September 2024 and new increases anticipated from September 2025), driving a £996.7k forecast overspend. Following these increases, the council has received requests from other colleges for rate increases, which are being reviewed but not yet included in the forecast.
findings.matters: Unquantified cost pressures from other colleges represent a downside risk to the forecast and signal sector-wide cost inflation the council cannot easily control or budget for.
findings.figures: Post-16 Element 3 Top-up overspend £996.7k; multiple colleges have submitted rate increase requests not yet quantified
findings.quote: Following the increase in hourly rates at The City of Portsmouth College, the authority has received requests from other colleges for an increase in hourly rates for the 2025-26 academic year. These are being reviewed but are not included in this forecast.

findings.paper_title: Dedicated Schools Grant 2025-2026 Quarter 2 Budget Monitoring
findings.headline: High Needs block forecast to overspend by £1.5m, driven by structural demand pressures.
findings.detail: The High Needs block is the main driver of the overall DSG overspend. findings.matters: Ring-fenced DSG deficits cannot be offset from the general fund and require government approval to recover from, making structural overspends a governance issue signalling underlying service cost inflation.

findings.paper_title: School Funding Arrangements 2026-2027
findings.headline: Council has contingency plans to adjust schools funding formula if allocation falls short of formula costs.

findings.committee: Cabinet Member for Children, Families and Education
findings.paper_title: School Funding Arrangements 2026-2027
findings.headline: High Needs Block remains under pressure with growing demand for EHCP support.
findings.detail: Portsmouth explicitly states its High Needs Block is under pressure, supporting increasing numbers of pupils with Education, Health and Care Plans through Element 3 Top-ups, backpack funding, Outreach and Sensory Impairment Services. The council proposes to transfer any surplus School Block funds (up to 0.5%) to High Needs Block to manage this growing demand.
findings.matters: EHCP provision is a statutory obligation with growing demand, creating recurring budget pressure. Transfers from other blocks are an indicator of sustained overspend against baselines in this service area.

findings.quote: The High Needs Block remains under pressure for 2025-26 and the authority is currently working on the forecasted expenditure for the 2026-27 budget, but any pressures will not be known until the publication of the funding allocation for 2026-27 in December 2025

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitorig 2025/2026 (Second Quarter) to end September 2025
findings.headline: Council warns demand pressures will force rising future savings requirements
findings.detail: The paper states: 'demand for services continues to place pressure or exacerbate known pressures. Consequently, there remains longer term uncertainty relating to further increases in demand. Should this persist, the Council's savings requirements in the future could rise.' This is a forward-looking warning that structural demand growth may force larger savings targets in coming years.
findings.matters: A finance director warning of potential future savings gaps suggests they expect sustained demand pressure and are signalling to members that further cuts may be needed. This is material to a lender assessing the council's ability to maintain service delivery under stress.
findings.figures: No specific figures but applies to Children, Families & Education (£1.8m) and Housing (£4.4m) overspends
findings.quote: demand for services continues to place pressure or exacerbate known pressures. Consequently, there remains longer term uncertainty relating to further increases in demand. Should this persist, the Council's savings requirements in the future could rise.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitorig 2025/2026 (Second Quarter) to end September 2025
findings.headline: Overall £1.035m overspend after contingency release signals structural budget gap
findings.detail: After releasing £4.45m from contingency to cover windfall costs, the council is still forecasting an overall overspend of £1.035m. This means even the contingency safety net is insufficient to absorb the year's variances, and the council will end the year behind budget.
findings.matters: An overspend in first half-year, even after using contingency, means the council is not tracking to a balanced outturn. This threatens reserves if it persists through year-end.
findings.figures: £1,034,900 net overspend after all transfers and contingency releases
findings.quote: Forecast Net Overspend 2025/26 1,035

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitorig 2025/2026 (Second Quarter) to end September 2025
findings.headline: Portfolio reserves depleted: Housing has zero balance to absorb future overspends
findings.detail: Housing & Tackling Homelessness is forecasting a £4.4m overspend but holds zero Portfolio Reserve. Under council policy, any year-end overspend not covered by reserve must be deducted from next year's cash limit. This means if homelessness demand remains high in 2026/27, the 2026/27 budget will automatically be cut by at least £4.4m to cover this year's overspend.
findings.matters: A portfolio with zero reserves and a structural overspend faces forced budget cuts next year. This creates cascading pressure and risks further service degradation in an already-stretched area.
findings.figures: Housing and Tackling Homelessness brought forward balance £0; forecast underspend £0; carried forward balance £0
findings.quote: where a Portfolio is presently forecasting a net overspend, in accordance with current Council policy, any overspending in 2025/26 which cannot be met by transfer from the Portfolio Specific Reserve will be deducted from cash limits in 2026/27

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitorig 2025/2026 (Second Quarter) to end September 2025
findings.headline: £4.45m released from Corporate Contingency in first half of year
findings.detail: The council is forecasting windfall costs totalling £4.45m that will be met from Corporate Contingency: homelessness (£4.05m), Spinnaker Tower lower profits (£0.30m), planning fees (£0.09m), and land charges (£0.01m). This is a substantial drawdown of contingency in Q2, leaving less buffer for Q3 and Q4.
findings.matters: Contingency reserves are the council's shock absorber. Using £4.45m in the first half of a financial year means less flexibility if unforeseen pressures emerge in Q3 or Q4.
findings.figures: £4,453,700 released from Corporate Contingency; homelessness £4,046,800, Spinnaker Tower £304,300, planning fees £88,600
